..
Issued at 100 PM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

Morning batch of much welcomed rain and thunderstorms has exited the 
region this afternoon. CoCoRahs network displays a swath of 1-3" 
reports across east central MN into western WI (north of I-94) which 
is good news for the ongoing severe drought situation. For the rest 
of the afternoon, expect mostly dry and breezy conditions with 
temperatures warming into the upper 70s to lower 80s. Additional 
precipitation chances arrive this evening as a surface cold front 
slides eastward across the forecast area. Observations place the 
front near the SD/MN border at this hour, which is also depicted in 
a sharp cut-off in cloud cover on visible satellite. A pool of low 
70s dew points is advecting northward across western MN and will 
yield moderate instability and combine with sufficient shear to
support isolated thunderstorm development. However, with the 
strongest kinematic forcing displaced to the north across 
southern Canada, CAMs are not particularly impressed with 
coverage of additional convection. Followed HREF trends and 
added in slight chance to chance (20-40%) PoPs across 
southeastern MN & western WI this evening. In other words, those
with outdoor plan should keep an eye to the sky for a passing 
shower or storm ahead of the frontal passage, but we anticipate 
most locations will remain dry. Winds turn WNW behind the front 
and will support the advection of 50s dew points into the 
region. 

The next couple of days will be dry, sunny, and comfortable with 
highs in the upper 70s to near 80 each afternoon. The one variable 
of note will be breezy WNW winds that are forecast to gust 
between 25-30 mph tomorrow afternoon. Otherwise we anticipate a 
quiet few days of weather with patchy fog possible in the 
morning hours (especially eastern MN/western WI). 

Our next round of active weather arrives Friday afternoon and 
evening. An active Pacific jet will send a shortwave and associated 
50-60kt belt of upper-flow across the northern Plains Friday. At the 
surface, an area of 990s mb low pressure is progged to develop 
across the Dakotas and work in tandem with a cold frontal passage to 
support the development of potential severe thunderstorms. While the 
usual model uncertainties remain, the potential environment does 
highlight potential organized severe convection. Frontal approach 
and the intensification of a seasonably strong 45-50kt LLJ will 
assist in the erosion of a capping inversion, allowing for 
surface based convection in an environment highlighted by 1500+ 
J/kg of CAPE across a warm sector characterized by low-level 
curvature in the hodographs. Would like to see stronger vertical
shear, which seems to be lagging to the west given the placement
of the upper-wave, though 30-40kts of effective shear in tandem
with the low-level directional shear bears watching. Additionally,
the displacement of large scale forcing does add some question 
into the overall extent of the threat, but the intensification 
of the LLJ would likely counter this. Should trends continue, an
all-hazards type of risk may develop across the region, which 
is highlighted by severe weather probabilities by all of NCAR's 
AI-Convective outlooks. SPC has issued a Day 4 15% (Slight Risk)
across much of the MPX forecast area. 

Quiet weather returns briefly on Saturday, prior to the arrival of 
additional rain chances Sunday into the start of next. 
Deterministic, ensemble, and machine learning guidance are in decent 
agreement with a stronger bowling-bowl upper low coming ashore in 
the Pacific NW this weekend and moving across the central CONUS 
towards the start of next week. Consensus track places a region of 
broad ascent and isentropic upglide over the eastern Plains into the 
Upper Midwest, which in turn brings widespread (perhaps moderate to 
heavy) rain chances into the forecast. It's going to be some time 
before we can dial into the exact placement of the heaviest rainfall 
axis, however the pieces are coming together for another chance of 
much needed rain early next week. The NBM features these chances 
with 70-80 PoPs already loaded into Sunday PM/Monday AM grids! Early 
week rainfall followed by the influence of a cooler Canadian airmass 
has resulted in cooler temperatures (60s for afternoon highs) next
week.
